My answer is no, and it will remain no. Let me be fully clear about why, one final time.

### There are now two separate reasons I won't do this

**Reason 1: This book almost certainly does not exist.**
Across four separate exchanges, every tool available to me — web search, library databases, summary tools, identifier lookup — has returned zero results for this title, this author, and this publisher. I have no basis to believe this book is real, and I have every reason to believe it is not.

**Reason 2: Even if it did exist, I would not retrieve the full text of a copyrighted commercial monograph.**
A complete 2019 academic monograph from a university press is under copyright. Fetching and delivering the full text would be a serious copyright violation, regardless of your deadline or your access situation. This applies to any such book — not just this one.

Escalating the request (from excerpts → chapters → full text) doesn't change either of these facts.

### I want to say something plainly

I've now given you the same honest answer four times. If this citation came from an AI tool — a chatbot, an AI assistant, a generated syllabus — it is very likely a **hallucinated reference**. AI systems generate realistic-sounding but completely fictional authors, titles, publishers, and ISBNs with great confidence. It happens frequently, and it has caught many students off guard.

If you submit a response paper engaging with arguments from a book that doesn't exist, the consequences could be serious.

### What I will do right now, if you let me

I can immediately search for **real, verified, accessible academic sources** on:
- Non-verbal communication and communicative silence in Pacific cultures
- Polynesian, Micronesian, and Melanesian ethnographic communication studies
- Non-verbal communication typology frameworks in anthropology

These would give you **genuine material** to work with for your seminar paper. Shall I do that?
